:::{#def-sample-space}
#### Sample space

The **sample space** of a random experiment, denoted $\Omega$,
is the [set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets-functions.html#def-set) of all of its possible outcomes.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-sample-space}
#### Sample space of a die roll

Rolling a six-sided die once has sample space $\Omega = \set{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-sigma-algebra}
#### $\sigma$-algebra

A **$\sigma$-algebra** on a set $S$
is a collection $\mathscr{S}$ of [subsets](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets-functions.html#def-subset) of $S$
that satisfies:

- $\mathscr{S}$ contains $S$ itself.
- For each set $A$ in $\mathscr{S}$,
  $\mathscr{S}$ contains its complement $S \setminus A$.
- For each sequence $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ of sets in $\mathscr{S}$,
  $\mathscr{S}$ contains their union $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Other sources call it a **$\sigma$-field**
(see [Wikipedia: $\sigma$-algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%CE%A3-algebra)).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-sigma-algebra}
#### $\sigma$-algebras for a die roll

For the die roll in @exm-sample-space,
the collection of all subsets of $\Omega = \set{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$,
since complements and unions of subsets of $\Omega$ are again subsets of $\Omega$.
So is the smaller collection

$$\set{\emptyset, \set{2, 4, 6}, \set{1, 3, 5}, \Omega}$$

which contains $\Omega$,
the complement of each of its sets,
and every union of its sets:
for example, $\set{2, 4, 6} \cup \set{1, 3, 5} = \Omega$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-sigma-algebra-closure}
#### Closure properties of a $\sigma$-algebra

If $\mathscr{S}$ is a [$\sigma$-algebra](#def-sigma-algebra) on a set $S$,
then $\mathscr{S}$ contains:

- the [empty set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets-functions.html#def-empty-set) $\emptyset$;
- the union $A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n$ of any finitely many sets $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ in $\mathscr{S}$;
- the intersection $\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i$ of any sequence $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ of sets in $\mathscr{S}$.

:::

::: proof

*Empty set.*
$\mathscr{S}$ contains $S$,
so it contains the complement of $S$,
which is $S \setminus S = \emptyset$.

*Finite unions.*
Extend $A_1, \ldots, A_n$ to a sequence
by setting $A_{n+1} = A_{n+2} = \cdots = \emptyset$;
each of these sets is in $\mathscr{S}$, by the first part.
Then:

$$
\ba
A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n
&= A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n \cup \emptyset \cup \emptyset \cup \cdots
&& \text{(a union with } \emptyset \text{ adds no elements)} \\
&= \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i
&& \text{(} A_i = \emptyset \text{ for } i > n \text{)}
\ea
$$

and $\mathscr{S}$ contains $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i$ by the union rule of @def-sigma-algebra.

*Countable intersections.*
An element of $S$ is in every $A_i$
exactly when it is in none of the complements $S \setminus A_i$,
so:

$$
\ba
\bigcap_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i
&= S \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} (S \setminus A_i)
&& \text{(De Morgan's law)}
\ea
$$

Each $S \setminus A_i$ is in $\mathscr{S}$ by the complement rule,
so their union is in $\mathscr{S}$ by the union rule,
and the complement of that union is in $\mathscr{S}$ by the complement rule again.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-power-set-sigma-algebra}
#### All subsets form a $\sigma$-algebra

For any set $S$,
the collection of all subsets of $S$
is a [$\sigma$-algebra](#def-sigma-algebra) on $S$.

:::

::: proof

Each condition of @def-sigma-algebra holds:

- $S$ is a subset of itself.
- For each subset $A$ of $S$,
  the complement $S \setminus A$ contains only elements of $S$,
  so it is a subset of $S$.
- For each sequence $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ of subsets of $S$,
  every element of $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i$ is in some $A_i$
  and so in $S$;
  the union is a subset of $S$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-event}
#### Event

An **event** is a subset of the [sample space](#def-sample-space) $\Omega$:
a set of outcomes.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

When $\Omega$ is uncountable, such as an interval of real numbers,
only the subsets in a designated [$\sigma$-algebra](#def-sigma-algebra) $\mathscr{S}$ on $\Omega$
count as events;
every set that arises in these notes is in $\mathscr{S}$.
When $\Omega$ is finite or [countably infinite](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/sets-functions.html#def-countably-infinite),
every subset of $\Omega$ can be an event,
because the collection of all subsets of $\Omega$ is a $\sigma$-algebra
(@thm-power-set-sigma-algebra),
as in @exm-sigma-algebra.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-event}
#### Rolling an even number

In @exm-sample-space,
the event "the roll is even" is $A = \set{2, 4, 6}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-occurs}
#### Occurrence of an event

An [event](#def-event) $A$ **occurs**
when the outcome of the experiment is in $A$,
and does not occur when the outcome is not in $A$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-occurs}
#### Rolling a 4

In @exm-event, if the die shows 4,
the event "the roll is even", $\set{2, 4, 6}$, occurs,
because $4 \in \set{2, 4, 6}$,
and the event "the roll is at most 2", $\set{1, 2}$, does not occur.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-complement}
#### Complement of an event

The **complement** of an [event](#def-event) $A$, denoted $\neg A$,
is the event that $A$ does not [occur](#def-occurs):
the set of outcomes in the sample space $\Omega$ that are not in $A$.

$$\neg A \eqdef \Omega \setminus A$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Other sources write $A^c$ or $\bar{A}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-complement}
#### Rolling an odd number

In @exm-event,
the complement of the event "the roll is even", $A = \set{2, 4, 6}$,
is the event "the roll is odd", $\neg A = \set{1, 3, 5}$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-mutually-exclusive}
#### Mutually exclusive events

Finitely or countably many sets $A_1, A_2, \ldots$,
such as [events](#def-event),
are **mutually exclusive**
(also called **disjoint**, **pairwise disjoint**, or **mutually disjoint**)
when no two of them share an element:

$$A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset \quad \text{for all } i \neq j$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-mutually-exclusive}
#### Low and high rolls

In @exm-sample-space,
the events "the roll is at most 2", $\set{1, 2}$,
and "the roll is at least 5", $\set{5, 6}$,
are mutually exclusive: no roll is in both.
The events "the roll is even", $\set{2, 4, 6}$,
and "the roll is at most 2", $\set{1, 2}$,
are not mutually exclusive: a roll of 2 is in both.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-partition}
#### Partition of an event

A **partition** of an [event](#def-event) $A$
is a finite or countably infinite collection of events $A_1, A_2, \ldots$
that satisfies:

- The events $A_1, A_2, \ldots$ are [mutually exclusive](#def-mutually-exclusive).
- Their union is $A$: $\bigcup_{i} A_i = A$.

A partition of the [sample space](#def-sample-space) is the case $A = \Omega$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Some sources also require each piece $A_i$ to contain at least one outcome.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-partition}
#### Partitioning the die roll

In @exm-sample-space,
the events "the roll is even", $\set{2, 4, 6}$,
and "the roll is odd", $\set{1, 3, 5}$,
are mutually exclusive, and their union is $\Omega$,
so they partition the sample space.
So do the six single-outcome events $\set{1}, \set{2}, \ldots, \set{6}$.
The events $\set{1, 2}$ and $\set{5, 6}$ from @exm-mutually-exclusive
do not partition $\Omega$: their union leaves out 3 and 4.

:::
